reason: The sources provide enough overlapping details to support a 45-second script with more than 10 backed claims.
story: Deep in the rugged Australian outback lies Spider Crater, a bizarre geological scar shaped like a giant arachnid. For decades following its discovery in the 1950s, scientists puzzled over its strange design. Some even proposed a volcanic past. But in the late 1970s, geologists found telltale fan-shaped fractures called shatter cones right in the center, proving it was carved by an ancient cosmic collision. The spiderlike legs are actually light-colored quartzite and sandstone ridges. They survived hundreds of millions of years of erosion while the surrounding rock wore away. Stretching roughly eleven by thirteen kilometers wide, the structure formed from a massive impact shockwave. Scientists estimate the event took place between nine hundred million and six hundred million years ago during the Precambrian era, leaving behind one of Earth's most visually striking impact scars.
angle: Spider Crater in Australia looks like a giant arachnid from space, carved not by biology, but by an ancient cosmic impact that left behind legs made of surviving stone ridges.

claims.claim: Spider Crater is located in the Kimberley region of northern Western Australia.
The unusual structure has been a puzzle since the 1950s.
Shatter cones were discovered in the center of the crater in the late 1970s.
Shatter cones are fan-shaped fractures that form only when intense shock waves travel through rock.
The full impact structure has an oval shape measuring about 13 kilometers by 11 kilometers.
The light-colored legs are sandstone and quartzite ridges that endured while other rock layers eroded away.
The central area bearing shatter cones is interpreted as the relic of a central uplift.
The impact event is estimated to have occurred between 900 million and 600 million years ago.
The site is effectively inaccessible due to very rugged terrain.
The name is derived from spider-like radiating ridges visibly prominent from the air or satellite images.

disputed: Some geologists concluded the projectile had a low angle trajectory from the north or northwest, while others suggested asymmetry was due to pre-existing topography. A script should attribute these differing views to geologists using phrases like 'according to some researchers'.
